name: Keystone
baseline: LLVM MC assembler (llvm-mc), the LLVM component Keystone is derived from
workload: Footprint and build cost of the assembler engine itself versus the full LLVM it was stripped from; the page gives no assembling-throughput comparison.
claimed_speedup: 'Keystone is more than 10 times smaller in size and in memory consumption' than LLVM; 'Initial verson of Keystone takes only 30 seconds to compile on a laptop, while LLVM needs 15 minutes to build.'
stars_or_usage: 2.6k stars; vcpkg port 'keystone', PyPI keystone-engine 0.9.2, crates.io keystone-engine bindings
tradeoffs: Dual licensed: GPL-2.0 only (no 'any later version', with a client exceptions file) or a paid royalty-free commercial licence for production use. Assembler only (no linker or compiler); accepts NASM/MASM-style input in addition to LLVM syntax; many architectures (Arm, Arm64, EVM, Hexagon, Mips, PowerPC, RISC-V, Sparc, SystemZ, X86). Because it is LLVM MC underneath, per-instruction assembling speed is not claimed to differ from llvm-mc.
caveats: The two numbers are footprint and build time of the library against building all of LLVM, not assemble time or output quality against GNU as, NASM or MASM. No benchmark code, compiler, flags or hardware ('on a laptop') are stated; the doc is first-party and from the 2016 launch ('Initial verson'). The same page lists the other differences (framework API, flexibility, code-and-data mixing) without measurements. Last commit before July 2026 was May 2023 (a build-compat fix), so releases are infrequent.
found_via: vcpkg ports list (versions/baseline.json, port 'keystone'); WebSearch 'crates.io assembler library benchmark vs keystone OR llvm-mc OR GNU as' surfaced docs/beyond_llvm.md

name: RASM (Z80 assembler)
baseline: Other Z80 assemblers: SjasmPlus (named in a CPCWiki search snippet), also vasm, SjASM, Pasmo; the README names no baseline ('the best alternatives')
workload: Assembling Z80 source (Amstrad CPC focus); the author's motivating project was a 512K cartridge of approx 350,000 words; throughput is quoted in instructions per second.
claimed_speedup: README: 'peak performance around 100 millions instructions per second', 'tens of millions instructions per second on a modern CPU', 'way faster than the best alternatives'. CPCWiki search snippet (page blocked here, not opened): '1 million lines in 0.03s ... 100x faster than SjasmPlus'.
stars_or_usage: 167 stars; README lists Arkos Tracker, R-GX, RetroDev and CPCSyntaxError as built on or embedding RASM
tradeoffs: Z80 only (Amstrad CPC, ZX Spectrum and similar), so it does not replace GNU as, NASM or MASM for x86. The whole assembler is one large C file (rasm.c) with bundled compression sources (zx7, lz4, exomizer, apultra, lzsa, salvador headers and directories). Command-line tool; builds on Linux, macOS, Windows, MS-DOS and MorphOS.
caveats: No benchmark script, input corpus, hardware or competitor version is in the repo. The README does not name the alternatives it beats; the SjasmPlus ratio comes from a CPCWiki snippet only. SjasmPlus's own README claims '1 million lines by 2-3 seconds', so the 100x figure compares two self-reported numbers (derived from page data and snippet). 'Instructions per second' is not directly comparable with lines per second.
found_via: WebSearch 'Z80 assembler fastest assembles speed benchmark RASM sjasmplus vasm pasmo lines per second' (CPCWiki and haiku-os depot snippets), then github.com/EdouardBERGE/rasm README

compiler_and_flags: cargo build --release --features bin (rustc version not stated); baselines are the distro /usr/bin/addr2line, eu-addr2line and llvm-addr2line packages, built by scripts/benchmark-addr2line-docker.sh in an openSUSE-based docker image (versions not stated)
name: addr2line (gimli-rs)
baseline: GNU binutils addr2line (also elfutils eu-addr2line and llvm-addr2line)
workload: Batch address-to-line lookups with `-af` on DWARF debug files: 500 random addresses in libxul.so and in clangd-18, 1000 in mold, 10000 in postgres; wall-clock mean from hyperfine (scripts/benchmark-addr2line.sh).
claimed_speedup: README: 'Current benchmarks show a performance improvement in all cases' (chart benchmark-time.svg, y axis 'Time [s]'). Bar heights read from the SVG (derived from page data; axis tick labels are not text), gimli versus llvm / binutils / eu: clangd-18 14.5 vs 31.1 / 232.2 / 172.8; libxul.so 8.0 vs 37.9 / 91.5 / 258.8; mold 11.2 vs 28.8 / 94.4 / 65.7; postgres 5.3 vs 6.3 / 14.0 / 151.7. That is about 1.2x to 4.7x faster than llvm-addr2line, 2.6x to 32x faster than binutils addr2line and 5.9x to 28x faster than eu-addr2line (derived from page data).
stars_or_usage: 429 stars; crates.io addr2line has about 541M downloads
tradeoffs: Trades memory for speed by caching parsed DWARF (lazy parsing where possible). Rust library plus a CLI that implements only part of GNU addr2line's options; not a C or C++ API. Needs debug info in DWARF.
caveats: Debug-info symbolization tool rather than an assembler, so the category fit is loose and the baseline is not in the category list. Hardware and tool versions are not stated, so this falls short of tier A. The sample addresses are produced by the crate's own CLI (`--all -a`, shuffled with a fixed seed). hyperfine is run with --min-runs=1, so slow baselines may be single runs. The SVG metadata is dated 2024-08-06 and may predate the 0.27 release. Ratios are read from bar heights in the SVG, not from tabulated values.
found_via: crates.io API search q=addr2line (crate addr2line); README Performance section, then scripts/benchmark-addr2line.sh and benchmark-time.svg

compiler_and_flags: target/release cargo build; Ropper and Capstone versions not stated
name: inspector-gadget
workload: Finding every gadget in an Android arm64 libmonochrome.so (Chrome and WebView library) and in a Windows x86_64 xul.dll, timed with `time`; disassembly via Capstone.
claimed_speedup: README: 'less than 10 seconds' (real 0m9.758s) for libmonochrome_64.so versus Ropper 'about 35 minutes'; xul.dll 'about a minute and a half' (real 1m25.907s) while Ropper was abandoned 'after about 3 hours'. About 215x and more than 125x (derived from page data).
tradeoffs: GPL-3.0. Depends on Capstone for decoding; covers arm, arm64, x86, x86_64, mips, mips64, ppc, ppc64, riscv, riscv64, sparc64 and s390x with PE/COFF, ELF and Mach-O parsing. De-duplicates and sorts gadgets (Ropper did not, per the README).
caveats: Single timed run per binary on an unspecified machine; the README's own TODO says 'collect better data and make some graphs'. The Ropper figures are anecdotal ('anecdotally ... run it overnight'), and the xul.dll Ropper run never finished, so only a lower bound exists. Ropper does extra work (semantic search, filtering), so the tools are not doing identical jobs. ROP-gadget search is binary-analysis tooling, so the category fit is loose and the baseline is not in the category list.
found_via: crates.io API search q='faster than capstone' (and 'rop gadget'); README Performance section

compiler_and_flags: Go 1.7.5 and 1.8.1; C compiler and flags not stated (benchmarks in test/ and cgocmp/)
name: c2goasm
baseline: cgo (calling the same C function through Go's C foreign-function interface)
workload: BenchmarkMultiplyAndAdd: one AVX2 float multiply-add function; the C compiler's assembly converted with c2goasm and called directly from Go versus the same C code called through cgo.
claimed_speedup: Go 1.7.5: 382 ns/op (cgo) to 10.9 ns/op (c2goasm), -97.15%; Go 1.8.1: 236 to 10.9 ns/op, -95.38%; README: cgo is 'still about 20x slower than directly calling into assembly code as wrapped by c2goasm'.
stars_or_usage: 1.3k stars; archived by the owner on 2021-12-01
tradeoffs: Converts C or C++ compiler assembly into Go (Plan 9) assembly, per function, amd64 only, with hand-written Go wrappers and an amd64.go declaration file; used with asm2plan9s. Not intended to port a whole project. Archived and read-only.
caveats: Measures call overhead on a trivially small function, not the quality of generated assembly, and says nothing against pure-Go code. Numbers come from Go 1.7.5 and 1.8.1 (2017); cgo overhead on current Go versions was not measured. Hardware and C compiler flags are not stated (the -12 name suffix suggests 12 procs, CPU model unknown). Assembly tooling in the Go ecosystem, not an assembler for the category's GNU as, NASM or MASM baselines.
found_via: Go module ecosystem check of assembly tooling (github.com/minio/c2goasm README section 'Benchmark against cgo'); compared with gorse-io/goat, mmcloughlin/avo and golang-asm READMEs, which carry no comparable numbers

name: NASM
workload: FFmpeg's x86 assembly build: NASM can emit dependency information as a side effect of assembling, Yasm needed a separate dependency pass.
claimed_speedup: FFmpeg commit 57b753b ('build: Prefer NASM assembler over YASM'): 'NASM is more actively maintained and permits generating dependency information as a sideeffect of assembling, thus cutting build times in half.'
stars_or_usage: 3.3k stars; preferred over Yasm by FFmpeg's build since the 2016 commit
tradeoffs: Intel-like syntax with many output formats; BSD 2-clause licence. Yasm's own README says it accepts both NASM and GAS syntaxes, so switching to NASM can mean porting GAS-syntax sources.
caveats: NASM is itself the incumbent named in the category's baseline list, so this entry only records its edge over Yasm. The claim is a commit message by an FFmpeg developer with no numbers, hardware or methodology, and it measures whole-project build time through dependency generation, not assemble speed or output quality. Not a general assembler benchmark.
found_via: WebSearch 'fast x86 assembler faster than NASM OR faster than GNU as OR faster than yasm assemble time benchmark' (FFmpeg mailing-list hit), then the FFmpeg commit page on github.com
